etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Latin criticus +‎ -al, from Ancient Greek κριτικός (kritikós, “of or for judging, able to discern”), from κρίνω (krínō, “I separate, judge”); also the root of crisis.

definitions.definition: Inclined to find fault or criticize.
Pertaining to, or indicating, a crisis or turning point.

quote.citation: 1892, Walter Besant, “Prologue: Who is Edmund Gray?”, in The Ivory Gate […], New York, N.Y.: Harper & Brothers, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: Such a scandal as the prosecution of a brother for forgery—with a verdict of guilty—is a most truly horrible, deplorable, fatal thing. It takes the respectability out of a family perhaps at a critical moment, when the family is just assuming the robes of respectability:  […]  it is a black spot which all the soaps ever advertised could never wash off.

quote.citation: 2013 September-October, Katie L. Burke, “In the News”, in American Scientist:
quote.text: Oxygen levels on Earth skyrocketed 2.4 billion years ago, when cyanobacteria evolved photosynthesis: […] . The evolutionary precursor of photosynthesis is still under debate, and a new study sheds light. The critical component of the photosynthetic system is the “water-oxidizing complex”, made up of manganese atoms and a calcium atom.

quote.citation: 2018, VOA Learning English > China's Melting Glacier Brings Visitors, Adds to Climate Concerns‎[1]:
quote.text: Third Pole glaciers are critical to billions of people from Vietnam to Afghanistan.

definitions.definition: Relating to criticism or careful analysis, such as literary or film criticism.

quote.citation: 2012 April 19, Alexandra Sifferlin, “‘Healthy’ Foods that Really Aren’t: Nutritionists Weigh In”, in Time‎[2]:
quote.text: “Unless you are purchasing cereal from a health food store, many brands that are marketed as healthy are usually full of sugar and processed ingredients,” says Garcia.  So when you’re choosing cereal, bread or any other whole-grain product, Garcia recommends reading labels with a critical eye.

definitions.definition: (medicine) Of a patient condition involving unstable vital signs and a prognosis that predicts the condition could worsen; or, a patient condition that requires urgent treatment in an intensive care or critical care medical facility.
(medicine, by extension) In such a condition.
Likely to go out of control if disturbed, that is, opposite of stable.
(physics) Of the point (in temperature, reagent concentration etc.) where a nuclear or chemical reaction becomes self-sustaining.
(physics) Of a temperature that is equal to the temperature of the critical point of a substance, i.e. the temperature above which the substance cannot be liquefied.

quote.citation: 1976, American Society of Mechanical Engineers, Journal of engineering for industry, volume 98, page 508:
quote.text: The second undamped system criticals show a greater percentage depression than the first.

quote.citation: 2008, John J. Coyle, C. John Langley, Brian Gibson, Supply Chain Management: A Logistics Perspective, page 564:
quote.text: Finally, criticals are high-risk, high-value items that give the final product a competitive advantage in the marketplace  […]  Criticals, in part, determine the customer's ultimate cost of using the finished product — in our example, the computer.

definitions.definition: In breakdancing, a kind of airflare move in which the dancer hops from one hand to the other.
